findings.what: The explanation carries 7 footnote marks and practice 5 more, 12 in all, and most sit on plain statements rather than a value he might look up: the lamps [^8], the bridge alarming [^7], symmetrical faults being common [^9], every detector being a path [^5], the zero side having a solid fault [^11], a partial short [^12] and the second-fault short [^13]. Keep [^3] (120 V DC) and [^4] (the 9.26 V case), perhaps one [^2], and drop the rest.

The working '220 × 16.7 ÷ 116.7 = 31.4 V' never says the positive's side is just its 100 kΩ arm, or that 116.7 is the two sides added. So the divider step is skipped on screen and only appears in the explanation. One short sentence fixes it, for example 'The positive's side is still 100 kΩ, so the sides add to 116.7 kΩ.'
'It reads 73.3 V' has no working (220 × 50 ÷ 150). At 91 words the screen also sits right at the ceiling, so cut the closing 10 MΩ sentence to make room for the working.

The picture stays on one detector with 'Negative to hull 31.4 V', which is the wrong answer '31.4 V, as with one detector'. A right Check plays nothing, so the picture never shows the 48.9 V cause. Either say in the stem that the picture shows one panel, or let a right Check show the second set of arms.

The puzzle is about a 100 V board with no detector, but the picture still shows screen 5's 220 V board with a solid negative fault, reading 220 V and 0 V. That clashes with the question. A neutral healthy picture would be better.

'On a ship, the automation and most other systems use a 24 V DC control voltage' sits between 'Many DC boards are insulated' and 'This 220 V board'. It reads as a non sequitur: it never says those 24 V systems are insulated, and the board in the picture is 220 V. Join it to the insulation point, for example 'Ships' 24 V DC control supplies are often run this way', or move it to screen 2's 24 V puzzle.

Five control groups sit between the picture and the four readout tiles. While a demonstration plays, the volts it names (100.0, 73.3, 31.4 V) are about a phone-screen below the bars. Put the readouts straight under the picture, or print each pole's volts beside its bar.
The bridge alarm lamp and the 'Meter: Ideal / 10 MΩ' status sit in the same rows as the symbol key. So the bridge's live lamp reads as a legend symbol rather than an indicator that lights.
When the monitor switches on, 'Off' swaps for the alarm lamp and 'Alarm' label at the midpoint of the 0.6 s move with no fade, while the needle fades in. It is a small pop-in.

'Only a monitor sees an equal fall on both' is absolute. An insulation test with the board dead, or a detector that switches in a known resistor, also sees it. Say 'the bridge and the voltmeter cannot see an equal fall on both; an injecting monitor can'.

The choice 'The voltmeter, switched pole to pole' means each pole to the hull. Practice's 'Then measure pole to pole' means across the bus. The same words carry two meanings, so screen 8 should say 'switched between the poles'.

'A slight difference points to a partial one' undersells a partial fault: screen 3's 20 kΩ partial leak gave 31.4 V against 188.6 V. Say that any split short of 0 V and the full bus points to a partial fault, and the bigger the split, the lower the leak.
'An older detector uses two lamps' adds an age the material does not give, since it calls this the simplest indicator. Say 'The simplest detector uses two lamps'.
The hint 'Work out 100 × 51 ÷ (500 + 51)' gives the whole sum, which is the answer. Hint at the rule instead: the negative takes its own resistance's share of the bus, out of both added.

Calling the board 'healthy' in the stem rules out 'Both poles have leaked to 20 kΩ' on its own, so the add-up test does none of the work. The hint for that choice also says equal leaks leave each pole at 110 V, but with the stem's old 20 kΩ meter they would read about 77.6 V. Drop 'healthy' and make the hint 'Equal leaks keep both readings equal, but they would still add to 220 V'.
The brief's lamp mode (Vertiv's two lamps in place of the arms) was not built. The lamps appear only in the explanation's words, so 'half brightness, then full on the healthy pole' is never seen.
